summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Reasner v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment against a former foster child who sued OCS over years of sexual abuse was vacated because a genuine factual dispute existed about when she discovered OCS's possible role, though her claim did not qualify for the extended limitations period of AS 09.10.065(a).
key_cases.relevance: Is Alaska's leading authority on the timeliness of a serious-harm claim by a child abused while in state care.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that a genuine factual dispute exists concerning when Reasner discovered information suggesting that OCS had played a role in allowing her to be abused.

key_cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services v. Mullins
key_cases.holding: A jury verdict holding OCS responsible for 95% of the damages suffered by two sisters abused by grandparents while in OCS legal custody was set aside as irrational, and OCS was granted a new trial on allocation of fault.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that OCS can be sued in negligence for harm to children in its legal custody, while limiting how much fault a jury may shift from the actual abuser.
key_cases.quote: Because the evidence supporting the jury's allocation of fault was so insubstantial as to make the verdict plainly unreasonable, we conclude that OCS is entitled to a new trial.

key_cases.case_name: Dapo v. State, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: In a former foster child's suit arising from abuse by his adoptive mother, the statute of repose applies to OCS's apportionment claim and is not unconstitutional as applied; dismissal of the apportionment claim was reversed and the case remanded.
key_cases.relevance: Concerns liability allocation for serious abuse suffered by a child the agency placed and whose adoption it approved.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the statute of repose applies to the apportionment claim and is not unconstitutional as applied.

key_cases.case_name: Blake J. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: A former foster child's suit over abuse by his adoptive mother was time-barred; neither OCS custody until age 19, collateral estoppel from an earlier guardianship competency ruling, nor equitable tolling saved the claim.
key_cases.relevance: Shows how severe-abuse claims by former foster children fail on timeliness even where the underlying harm is undisputed.
key_cases.quote: collateral estoppel is not available here because the competency standard in a conservatorship and partial guardianship proceeding is different from the standard of competence necessary to file suit

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative federal constitutional duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence, so a caseworker's failure to remove a child who is later injured by a parent is not itself a § 1983 due-process violation.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why a child's death or serious injury at a caregiver's hands generally cannot be redressed as a federal due-process claim, pushing families toward Alaska state-law negligence theories.
key_cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

extended_foster_care_age: To the 21st birthday by court order only: state custody ends at the 19th birthday unless the court grants one-year extensions past 19, which require the person's consent and a best-interests finding, and a person already released from care may ask the court to resume custody before the 21st birthday (Alaska Stat. § 47.10.080(c)(1)(B), § 47.10.080(v), § 47.10.100(a))

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
